seoTitle: Warren Medical Malpractice Lawyer: Two-Year Deadline, Notice of Intent, 2026 Caps, and Who the Defendant Is
seoDescription: Harmed by a doctor, hospital, or clinic in Warren? Michigan malpractice law has a two-year deadline, a 182-day notice before suit, a sworn expert affidavit, and a cap on pain-and-suffering damages ($596,400 or $1,065,000 in 2026). How the rules apply to Henry Ford Warren Hospital, the Macomb County hospitals, surgery centers, and federally funded clinics. Free review. (313) 406-7606.
tagline: Michigan gives a malpractice victim two years, not three, and requires a written notice and an expert’s sworn affidavit before suit. In Warren the first question is who employed the provider, because the hospital on Twelve Mile changed hands in 2024.

c.v: A medical malpractice claim in Michigan has rules no other injury claim has: a two-year deadline instead of three; a written Notice of Intent served on each provider at least 182 days before suit; a sworn Affidavit of Merit from a qualified expert filed with the complaint; strict rules on who that expert can be; and a cap on pain-and-suffering damages. A case that misses any one of them can be lost before its merits are heard. In Warren there is a question to answer first: who the defendant is. The hospital on Twelve Mile changed hands in 2024. The emergency physician who saw you may work for the hospital or for a separate group. The specialist or surgery center on Van Dyke or Twelve Mile may be independent, physician-owned, or part of a health system. And a clinic funded by the federal government is sued under federal law, on a different clock, in a different court.

sections.heading: What malpractice is, and is not

c.v: A bad outcome is not malpractice. Malpractice is a bad outcome caused by a provider who failed to do what a reasonably competent provider in the same specialty would have done in the same circumstances (MCL 600.2912a). You must prove the standard of care, a breach, that the breach more likely than not caused the injury, and damages. Michigan requires proof that the patient would have had a better outcome; a lost chance of a better outcome is compensable only where that chance was greater than 50 percent (MCL 600.2912a(2)). A qualified physician’s written review of the records decides, before anything is filed, whether a case exists. Many do not, and we say so.

sections.heading: Warren’s providers, and who answers for each

c.v: The hospital on Twelve Mile Road was Ascension Macomb-Oakland Hospital’s Warren campus until October 1, 2024, when it became part of a joint venture operated by Henry Ford Health, which owns 80 percent, with Ascension holding the rest. Some firm pages still use the old name. For a claim, the change matters in two ways: records for care before and after that date may sit with different custodians, and the correct legal entity for the Notice of Intent must be identified from current corporate filings, not from the sign. Claims against the hospital and its employed providers are filed in the Sixteenth Judicial Circuit Court in Mount Clemens.
Emergency physicians and other contracted groups.

Many hospitals staff their emergency departments, anesthesia, and radiology through separate physician groups. The Notice of Intent must name the group as well as the hospital. Where a patient came to the hospital for care and reasonably believed the doctor worked for it, Michigan law can hold the hospital responsible under ostensible agency. The case that established the rule,
Grewe v Mt Clemens General Hospital
(1978), arose at a Macomb County hospital.

Henry Ford Macomb in Clinton Township and McLaren Macomb in Mount Clemens (claims in the Sixteenth Circuit); Corewell Health William Beaumont University Hospital in Royal Oak (Sixth Circuit, Pontiac); and the Detroit hospitals across Eight Mile (Third Circuit). The venue follows where the malpractice occurred and where the defendants are (MCL 600.1629).
Surgery centers, imaging centers, and physician offices.

Warren has outpatient surgery centers, a surgical hospital, imaging centers, urgent care clinics, and many primary-care and specialty practices, some physician-owned, some independent, and some owned by a health system. A delayed diagnosis in an office practice and a surgical complication at an outpatient center are frequent claims, and the employer of each provider who touched the chart must be identified. Michigan rules apply.

Health centers that receive federal Health Center Program funding can have their providers deemed federal employees for malpractice purposes. A claim against one follows the Federal Tort Claims Act, not Michigan procedure: an administrative claim on Standard Form 95 to the Department of Health and Human Services within two years (28 USC 2401(b)), no Notice of Intent, and suit in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan, tried to a judge without a jury. Identifying a deemed clinic early is the difference between a timely claim and none.

faqs.question: How long do I have to sue a Warren doctor or hospital?

answer.v: Two years from the malpractice, with a six-month discovery rule capped at six years. Because the Notice of Intent must be served 182 days before suit and the expert review comes first, call well inside the first year.

faqs.question: The hospital was Ascension Macomb-Oakland when I was treated. Does the name change affect my claim?

answer.v: Not the claim itself, but it affects who is named. Care before and after October 1, 2024 may involve different legal entities and records custodians, and the Notice of Intent must go to the right one.

faqs.question: The emergency doctor did not work for the hospital. Can I still bring a claim against the hospital?

answer.v: Sometimes. Michigan recognizes ostensible agency: if you went to the hospital for care and reasonably believed the doctor was the hospital’s, the hospital can be responsible. The physician’s group is named as well.

faqs.question: My care was at a community health center. Is that different?

answer.v: It may be. If the center is federally funded and its providers are deemed federal employees, the claim is against the United States under the Federal Tort Claims Act: an administrative claim within two years, no Notice of Intent, and suit in federal court without a jury. We check the center’s status at the first call.

faqs.question: Is there a cap on what I can recover?

answer.v: On pain-and-suffering damages only: $596,400 in the standard case and $1,065,000 for the catastrophic permanent injuries the statute lists, in 2026, adjusted each year. Medical bills, lost earnings, and future care are not capped.

faqs.question: My child was injured at birth. How long do we have?

answer.v: A child injured before age eight has until the tenth birthday to file. The parents’ own claims are subject to the ordinary two-year period, so the family should not wait.
